newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Annan names African envoys for Congo rights probe.
newsitem.headline: Annan names African envoys for Congo rights probe.

text.p: The United Nations named a Togolese Supreme Court judge and Zimbabwean prosecutor on Friday to head a new probe of alleged massacres of Rwandan refugees in President Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of the Congo.

But U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, in a statement, did not give a starting date for the mission, which has been delayed for two months because of Kabila's objections to the previous team leader, Roberto Garreton of Chile, who had publicised reports of the massacres.
The head of the team is Atsu-Koffi Amega of Togo, who has considerable experience in the complicated Rwandan civil war.

Also named was Andrew Chigovera, the deputy attorney general of Zimbabwe, a member of the U.N. Committee on Racial Discrimination. Annan said a third member of the team would be announced within a few days.

Amega was former president of the Togolese Supreme Court and headed a U.N. Security Council investigation of the 1994 genocide in Rwanda of Tutsis and moderate Hutus by militant Hutus. He also led a U.N. fact-finding mission to Nigeria in 1996 on the trial and execution of author Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other minority rights activists.
In blunt language he told a news conference in Lagos a year ago, "In this country as I have seen it, the problems of human rights are terrible. The political problems are terrifying."

After the genocide in Rwanda, more than a million Rwandan Hutus crossed into what was then Zaire, fearing reprisals by Tutsis who have taken over the government. Most returned home, but U.N. relief officials say up to 200,000 are still roaming in the region or dead.

Kabila's forces, aided by Rwanda, seized power in Kinshasa in May, deposing veteran president Mobutu Sese Seko, after a whirlwind military campaign across the vast Central African state. He denied his Tutsi supporters were responsible for the massacres.

Garreton angered the Congo ruler by releasing two critical reports of massacres by his followers based on witnesses. Rights groups said his replacement would set a precedent and Burundi last month rejected a U.N. investigation by Paulo Sergio Pinheiro, a noted Brazilian human rights expert.
But U.N. officials at the time stressed the Congo situation was an exception and was approved by Security Council members to get around the deadlock.

U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson, who also gave in to Kabila's demands when he visited the country, was instrumental in getting Annan to organise his own investigation, thereby temporarily sparing the Congo possible international isolation.
